messages.subject: Models with no adjustments
parts:
Distance Samplers

I’m analysing the auditory contacts of tropical forest parrots
from point counts (non flying contacts only). After data truncation
to 70m to overcome cluster size bias, I’m left with 106 observations
and my best model is a Uniform key with no adjustments. Analysis
details are:
Model: Uniform key (6 intervals)
Chi-sq.: 3.88; P=0.57;
%CV: 13.51
Essentially, my detection function assumes that if this species
called at any distance up to 70m I was equally likely to contact it.
The species being a typically noisy parrot, and my being familiar
with this species, I am happy that this assumption was fulfilled.
The Chi-sq indicates a good fit to the data and density estimates are
precise. I can’t see any problems (it is, after all, just truncation
at the end of the usual hard shoulder) however, are there any
reasons that such a model may be ‘unstable’ or overly sensitive and
thus yield spurious results?

With regard to cluster size problems, whilst DISTANCE assumes accurate
cluster estimation there are obvious problems of underestimation of
cluster size with distance from the point. However, in addition I can
see that there may also be situations where the opposite is true,
that, with increasing distance, there could be a tendency to lump
single observations together as clusters. A much simplified example
is, if two individuals are 30m apart, one at 0m one at 30m from the
observer then these may get recorded as two separate observations. At
100m from the observer two individuals 30m apart are likely to get
recorded as a single observation of cluster size 2 despite being the
same distance apart. Closer to the observer one is better able to
make decisions on whether individuals belong to the same cluster.
Has anyone attempted to model how this may bias results?

Cheers
Jon Walker
